title: Evolution
summary: Descent with modification: mechanisms, evidence, history and origins.

layers.basics: Evolution is change in the inherited traits of populations over generations. Natural selection, drift, mutation and gene flow drive it, and all life shares common ancestry.
layers.deeper: Fossils, DNA, anatomy and geography all point to the same tree of life. New species form when populations become reproductively isolated, and the history of life is punctuated by mass extinctions and radiations.
layers.expert: Modern evolutionary theory integrates population genetics, development and phylogenetics. Open questions include the origin of life, the tempo of macroevolution and the role of non-genetic inheritance.

open_questions: How important non-genetic inheritance and developmental bias are in adaptation is debated.
How the tempo of large-scale change (gradual versus punctuated) varies among lineages is still being studied.

title: Natural selection

layers.basics: Individuals vary, some traits are heritable, and more offspring are born than can survive. Those with helpful traits leave more offspring, so such traits spread.
layers.deeper: Darwin and Wallace proposed the idea in 1858–59. Fitness is relative reproductive success, not strength.
layers.expert: Selection acts on phenotypes but changes allele frequencies: Δp = p(w̄ₐ − w̄)/w̄. The Price equation generalises it; the response to selection is R = h²S.

facts: dark form first recorded 1848; it became the common form by the late 1800s

title: Modes of selection and adaptation

layers.basics: Directional selection favours one extreme, stabilising favours the middle and disruptive favours both extremes.
layers.deeper: Human birth weight is under stabilising selection; beak size in Galápagos finches shifted after a severe drought, because large-beaked birds survived best (Grants' studies).
layers.expert: Frequency-dependent and balancing selection maintain variation (MHC, sickle-cell). Adaptations differ from exaptations, and not every trait is an adaptation (Gould & Lewontin "spandrels").

facts: a few percent deeper in the next generation (Daphne Major, 1977)

title: Sexual selection

layers.basics: Traits like peacock tails and antlers evolve because they help in winning mates, even at a cost to survival.
layers.deeper: Female choice and male–male competition are the two main mechanisms.
layers.expert: Handicap and good-genes models explain costly ornaments; Fisherian runaway selection explains exaggerated traits. Sperm competition and sexual conflict drive rapid evolution of reproductive proteins.

open_questions: How much female choice reflects indirect genetic benefits versus runaway or sensory-bias processes is debated.

title: Evidence for evolution

layers.basics: Fossils show change over time, homologous structures (the forelimb of a bat and a whale) show common ancestry, and DNA sequences nest into a tree.
layers.deeper: Vestigial structures and shared pseudogenes (e.g., the broken vitamin C gene GULO in humans, apes, monkeys and tarsiers, but not in lemurs) fit descent. Observed evolution includes antibiotic resistance and Lenski's E. coli.
layers.expert: Independent trees from morphology and molecules agree; transitional fossils (Tiktaalik, Archaeopteryx) fill predicted gaps. Lenski's experiment has run since 1988 (> 75,000 generations).

facts: ≈ 98.8% for aligned single-base differences (lower when insertions and deletions are counted)

title: Species concepts

layers.basics: The biological species concept defines a species as interbreeding populations reproductively isolated from others.
layers.deeper: Alternatives include morphological, phylogenetic and ecological concepts. Bacteria and asexual organisms fit poorly with the biological concept.
layers.expert: Ring species and hybrid zones show that reproductive isolation can build up in degrees, so species boundaries are often blurry. One model-based estimate (Mora et al. 2011) puts the number of eukaryotic species at about 8.7 million (± 1.3 million), with only ≈ 1.2–2 million described.

open_questions: No single species concept works for all life; the boundaries are a matter of convention in many groups.

layers.basics: Populations separated by a barrier (allopatric) diverge until they can no longer interbreed. Speciation can also occur without barriers (sympatric), such as by polyploidy.
layers.deeper: Prezygotic barriers (timing, behaviour, mechanical) and postzygotic barriers (hybrid sterility, inviability) keep species apart.
layers.expert: Dobzhansky–Muller incompatibilities accumulate in isolation. Polyploid speciation is common in plants. Speciation can take from a few generations (polyploids) to millions of years.

title: Adaptive radiation and coevolution

layers.basics: When a lineage enters a new environment with open niches it can split into many species, like Darwin's finches and Hawaiian honeycreepers.
layers.deeper: Coevolution is reciprocal evolutionary change in interacting species, such as flowers and pollinators or hosts and parasites.
layers.expert: Radiations often follow key innovations or mass extinctions (mammals after the Cretaceous). Red Queen dynamics describe perpetual arms races between hosts and parasites.

facts: ≈ 18 species (17 on the Galápagos, 1 on Cocos Island)

layers.basics: A phylogenetic tree shows branching ancestry. A clade includes an ancestor and all its descendants.
layers.deeper: Characters shared because of a common ancestor (synapomorphies) define clades; similarity from convergent evolution (analogy) misleads.
layers.expert: Cladistic methods use parsimony or probabilistic models. Monophyletic, paraphyletic and polyphyletic groups are distinguished; "reptiles" excluding birds is paraphyletic.

title: Molecular clocks and divergence times

layers.basics: If mutations accumulate at a steady rate, the number of differences between species estimates how long ago they split.
layers.deeper: Clocks are calibrated with fossils. Human and chimp lineages split about 6–8 million years ago (estimates vary).
layers.expert: Rates vary between lineages (relaxed clocks) and with generation time; Bayesian dating (BEAST) integrates calibrations. Rate heterogeneity gives wide credible intervals.

facts: ≈ 0.5–1 × 10⁻⁹ per site per year (depends on method)
open_questions: Pedigree-based mutation rates and fossil-calibrated substitution rates differ by about a factor of two, so deep divergence dates remain uncertain.

title: Geologic time and the history of life

layers.basics: Earth is ≈ 4.54 billion years old. Life appeared by ≈ 3.5–3.8 billion years ago, animals by ≈ 575 million, and humans only in the last ≈ 300,000 years.
layers.deeper: Key events: oxygenation (≈ 2.4 Ga), eukaryotes (≈ 1.6–2 Ga), Cambrian explosion (≈ 540 Ma), land plants (≈ 470 Ma), dinosaurs (≈ 230–66 Ma).
layers.expert: Radiometric dating (U–Pb, K–Ar) calibrates the timescale. Banded iron formations, stromatolites and biomarkers document early life; Ediacaran biota precede the Cambrian.

title: Mass extinctions

layers.basics: Five mass extinctions wiped out most species, including the end-Permian event (≈ 252 Ma), which killed roughly 80–95% of marine species (estimates vary), and the end-Cretaceous event (≈ 66 Ma). The others were end-Ordovician, Late Devonian and end-Triassic.
layers.deeper: Causes include volcanism, climate change, ocean anoxia and, for the dinosaurs, an asteroid impact at Chicxulub.
layers.expert: Recovery takes ≈ 5–10 million years. Many scientists argue we are entering a sixth mass extinction, but this is debated: estimates of current extinction rates run from about 100 to 1,000 times the background rate.

open_questions: Whether current extinctions amount to a sixth mass extinction depends on how background rates and undescribed species are estimated; published multipliers range from about 100 to about 1,000.

title: Macroevolution and evo-devo
summary: Big changes and the genes behind body plans.

layers.basics: Large-scale changes arise by the accumulation of small ones, plus changes in genes that control development.
layers.deeper: Hox genes pattern the body axis in animals; small regulatory changes can alter limbs, eyes or body segments. Whale limbs and bird wings show repurposing.
layers.expert: Evo-devo studies modular regulatory evolution and deep homology (Pax6 for eyes). Punctuated equilibrium proposes stasis with bursts of change; the fossil record supports both tempo patterns in different lineages.

facts: 4 (39 genes in humans); most teleost fishes have 7–8
eye development in flies and mice
open_questions: How often large body-plan changes come from regulatory versus protein changes, and how common punctuated patterns are, is still being worked out.

title: Neutral and nearly neutral theory

layers.basics: Most mutations that persist in a genome are effectively neutral and spread through drift rather than selection.
layers.deeper: Kimura proposed the neutral theory in 1968. It underlies molecular clocks.
layers.expert: For strictly neutral mutations the substitution rate equals the neutral mutation rate (k = μ), independent of population size, because the 2N·μ new mutants per generation each fix with probability 1/(2N). Nearly neutral dynamics depend on Ne·s; how much of genome evolution is selected remains actively debated.

open_questions: The proportion of genomic divergence driven by positive selection versus drift is still disputed.

title: Kin selection and altruism

layers.basics: Animals may help relatives because relatives share genes. Worker bees and meerkat helpers are examples.
layers.deeper: Hamilton's rule says altruism evolves when relatedness × benefit exceeds cost.
layers.expert: rb > c, where r is relatedness. Haplodiploidy makes full sisters r = 0.75 if the queen mated once. It is no longer seen as the main driver of eusociality: many eusocial species are diploid, and queens of many haplodiploid species mate with several males. The role of kin selection versus group selection is still debated.

open_questions: Whether kin selection or group selection better explains the evolution of eusociality is debated.

title: Human evolution
summary: The primate lineage leading to us.

layers.basics: Humans share ancestors with the African apes. The hominin line includes Australopithecus (e.g. "Lucy", ≈ 3.2 Ma), early Homo (≈ 2.8 Ma) and Homo sapiens (≈ 300,000 years ago in Africa).
layers.deeper: Bipedalism came early, large brains later. Neanderthals and Denisovans interbred with modern humans; most non-Africans carry ≈ 1–2% Neanderthal DNA.
layers.expert: Ancient DNA has reshaped the story: multiple dispersals, admixture and local adaptation (lactase persistence, high altitude EPAS1). Details of the Out-of-Africa timing and the role of archaic admixture in Africa remain under active study.

open_questions: Whether H. sapiens arose in one part of Africa or from several interconnected African populations (African multiregionalism) is debated, as is the branching of early Homo lineages.

title: Origin of life

layers.basics: Life likely began on early Earth more than 3.5 billion years ago from chemical reactions that formed organic molecules, which then organised into self-copying systems.
layers.deeper: Leading ideas: RNA world, metabolism-first at hydrothermal vents, and lipid vesicle protocells. Miller–Urey (1953) made amino acids from simple gases.
layers.expert: No complete pathway is known. Challenges: chirality, polymerisation in water, and the origin of coding. Prebiotic synthesis of nucleotides (Sutherland 2009) suggests plausible routes; none has produced a full cell from chemistry.

facts: Earliest widely accepted fossil evidence of life
≈ 3.5 Ga (older claims up to ≈ 4.1 Ga are disputed)
open_questions: Whether life began as RNA, metabolism, lipids or something else is unresolved.
Where it began (vents, ponds, clay surfaces) is not settled.
How information-bearing polymers first arose without enzymes is unknown.

title: RNA world and the last universal common ancestor

layers.basics: The RNA world hypothesis proposes that RNA both stored information and catalysed reactions before DNA and proteins.
layers.deeper: Ribozymes support the idea: the ribosome itself is an RNA enzyme. LUCA, the last common ancestor of all living cells (bacteria and archaea, with eukaryotes arising later from within the archaea), is estimated at roughly 4.2 billion years ago in one recent study (4.09–4.33 billion years, Moody et al. 2024); other estimates are younger.
layers.expert: Reconstructions suggest LUCA was probably an anaerobic, hydrogen-using cell, possibly with a Wood–Ljungdahl pathway, though reconstructions differ. In vitro evolution has produced RNA polymerase ribozymes that copy short templates.

open_questions: Whether an RNA world preceded DNA/protein life is unproven.
The complexity and habitat of LUCA are contested.

layers.basics: Individuals do not evolve; populations do. Evolution has no goal, and "survival of the fittest" means reproductive success, not strength.
layers.deeper: Humans did not evolve from today's chimps; both share an ancestor. "Theory" in science means a well-tested explanation.
layers.expert: Evolution is not progress towards complexity. Adaptation is limited by history, trade-offs and chance; many traits are compromises or by-products.

layers.basics: Researchers grow microbes or flies for hundreds or thousands of generations under controlled conditions and watch them adapt.
layers.deeper: In Lenski's experiment, one of the 12 E. coli populations evolved the ability to use citrate at about 31,500 generations. The other 11 did not, which shows the role of chance and history.
layers.expert: Samples of each population are frozen every 500 generations, so researchers can restart evolution from an earlier point and replay it. In replays, the citrate trait arose far more often from later samples than from early ones, which suggests that an earlier "potentiating" mutation made it possible (Blount 2008).

title: Diversity of life
summary: Fungi, protists, plants and animals, from invertebrates to vertebrates.

layers.basics: Life on Earth is enormously diverse. This section tours the major groups of eukaryotes: fungi, algae, plants and animals, with their body plans and lifestyles.
layers.deeper: Groups are defined by shared ancestry. Key transitions include multicellularity, the move to land, the evolution of seeds and flowers, and of backbones, jaws, limbs, feathers and fur.
layers.expert: Phylogenomics keeps revising animal and plant relationships (e.g., placement of ctenophores or sponges at the base of animals). Diversity gradients and extinction risk are explored in ecology and conservation.

layers.basics: Fungi are mostly made of threads (hyphae) forming a mycelium. They absorb food from their surroundings after digesting it with enzymes.
layers.deeper: Major groups: chytrids, the former "zygomycetes" (now split into several lineages), ascomycetes (yeasts, molds, morels) and basidiomycetes (mushrooms). Fungi are more closely related to animals than to plants.
layers.expert: The largest known organism by area is an Armillaria ostoyae mycelium in Oregon's Malheur National Forest (≈ 9.6 km²; at least 2,400 years old and possibly much older). Fungi reproduce both sexually and asexually, and many have long dikaryotic stages.

layers.basics: Fungi decompose dead matter, form mycorrhizae with plant roots, and make lichens with algae or cyanobacteria. Some cause disease in plants and animals.
layers.deeper: Most land plant species (roughly 70–90%, depending on the survey) form mycorrhizae, partnerships with fungi that trade soil minerals for sugar. Yeasts bring us bread and beer, and the mould Penicillium gave us penicillin, the first widely used antibiotic.
layers.expert: Chytrid fungus Batrachochytrium has caused amphibian declines in > 500 species. White-nose syndrome has killed millions of bats. Fungal disease is estimated to be involved in about 3.8 million deaths a year (Denning 2024), though often alongside another serious illness, so the number caused by the fungus alone is smaller.

title: Algae and the origin of land plants
summary: Green algae are the closest relatives of land plants.

layers.basics: Land plants descended from streptophyte green algae (charophytes). The oldest fossil land-plant spores are about 470 million years old, and molecular clocks place the split from the algae earlier.
layers.deeper: Moving onto land needed protection from drying (cuticle), support, and water transport.
layers.expert: Streptophyte algae share cell-division and cell-wall features with plants; Most genome-scale analyses favour Zygnematophyceae as the sister group, though some studies recover other groups. Key innovations: sporopollenin, embryos, vascular tissue.

open_questions: Which streptophyte algal group is the sister of land plants, and when land plants arose, are still tested with new genomes.

layers.basics: Mosses, liverworts and hornworts have no true vascular tissue and stay small. Ferns and lycophytes have vascular tissue but still need water for sperm to swim.
layers.deeper: These plants have alternation of generations: a gametophyte stage and a sporophyte stage. In mosses the gametophyte dominates; in ferns the sporophyte does.
layers.expert: Carboniferous seedless forests formed much of today's coal. Ferns number ≈ 10,500 species; vascular tissue with lignin evolved ≈ 430 Ma.

title: Gymnosperms and angiosperms

layers.basics: Seeds protect and feed the embryo. Gymnosperms (conifers, cycads, ginkgo, gnetophytes) have "naked" seeds, often in cones; angiosperms (flowering plants) enclose seeds in fruit.
layers.deeper: Angiosperms are ≈ 300,000 species. Double fertilisation produces an embryo and nutritive endosperm. Flowers attract animals for pollination.
layers.expert: Flowering plants appear in the fossil record in the Early Cretaceous and diversified rapidly, which Darwin called an "abominable mystery". Molecular clocks suggest an older origin, and the timing is still debated. Basal lineages include Amborella. Monocots and eudicots differ in cotyledons, vascular arrangement and pollen apertures.

open_questions: When flowering plants first arose is debated: the fossil record and molecular clocks give different answers.

title: Animal features and body plans
summary: What makes an animal and how animals are organised.

layers.basics: Animals are multicellular heterotrophs without cell walls that develop from an embryo. Body plans differ in symmetry, layers and body cavity.
layers.deeper: Radial vs bilateral symmetry, diploblastic vs triploblastic layers, and protostome vs deuterostome development are the main categories.
layers.expert: Molecular phylogeny groups bilaterians into Lophotrochozoa, Ecdysozoa and Deuterostomia. Whether sponges or ctenophores branch first remains debated.

open_questions: Whether sponges or comb jellies are sister to all other animals is unsettled.

layers.basics: Sponges filter water through pores and have no true tissues. Cnidarians (jellyfish, corals, anemones) have stinging cells and radial symmetry.
layers.deeper: Coral reefs, built by cnidarians with symbiotic algae, cover well under 1% of the sea floor but host a disproportionate share of marine species (a quarter is a widely quoted but uncertain figure, and many reef species are undescribed).
layers.expert: Cnidocytes fire nematocysts in ≈ 700 ns, among the fastest cellular events. Coral bleaching occurs when symbionts are expelled under heat stress.

title: Flatworms, mollusks and annelids

layers.basics: Flatworms include free-living planarians and parasitic tapeworms and flukes. Mollusks have a muscular foot, mantle and often a shell; annelids are segmented worms.
layers.deeper: Octopuses are mollusks with large brains and ≈ 500 million neurons. Earthworms aerate soil.
layers.expert: Cephalopods have closed circulatory systems and camera-type eyes arising independently of vertebrates. Whether segmentation in annelids, arthropods and vertebrates evolved independently or descends from a segmented ancestor is unresolved; some shared genetic machinery may be deeply homologous.

open_questions: Whether body segmentation evolved once or several times in animals is unresolved.

title: Nematodes and arthropods
summary: Molting animals: roundworms and jointed-legged animals.

layers.basics: Nematodes are unsegmented roundworms found nearly everywhere. Arthropods (insects, spiders, crustaceans) have jointed legs and a chitin exoskeleton.
layers.deeper: Arthropods make up ≈ 80% of described animal species. Moulting lets them grow despite the rigid exoskeleton.
layers.expert: Ecdysozoa moult under ecdysone control. The arthropod body plan has repeated segments modified by Hox genes into specialised appendages.

title: Insects and entomology basics

layers.basics: Insects have three body regions, six legs and usually wings. They pollinate crops, spread diseases and decompose waste.
layers.deeper: Complete metamorphosis (egg, larva, pupa, adult) occurs in beetles, flies, butterflies and bees; incomplete metamorphosis in grasshoppers.
layers.expert: Beetles alone are ≈ 400,000 described species. Social insects (ants, termites, bees) show eusociality with castes. Long-term monitoring finds land insect abundance falling by about 9% per decade on average in one large analysis (van Klink 2020), though trends vary a lot by place and group.

facts: Leading crop types that benefit from animal pollination

title: Echinoderms and chordates

layers.basics: Echinoderms (sea stars, urchins) have radial adult symmetry; chordates have a notochord, dorsal nerve cord, pharyngeal slits and a post-anal tail at some stage.
layers.deeper: Tunicates and lancelets are invertebrate chordates. Vertebrates add a backbone and a skull.
layers.expert: Echinoderms and hemichordates form a clade (Ambulacraria) that is the sister group of the chordates. Vertebrate genomes show two rounds of whole-genome duplication near the origin of vertebrates, though details of their number and timing are still debated.

open_questions: The number and timing of whole-genome duplications near the origin of vertebrates are still debated.

layers.basics: Fishes (jawless, cartilaginous, ray-finned, lobe-finned) are the oldest vertebrates. Amphibians moved to land but most still need water or damp places to breed.
layers.deeper: Tetrapods evolved from lobe-finned fishes ≈ 375 Ma (Tiktaalik). Amphibian skin breathes and is sensitive to pollution.
layers.expert: Ray-finned fishes are the great majority (about 96–99%, depending on the count) of fish species (≈ 35,000); the rest are sharks and rays, jawless fishes and lobe-finned fishes. Frogs' decline is among the fastest of any vertebrate group (≈ 40% of species threatened).

layers.basics: Reptiles have scaly skin and mostly lay shelled eggs on land. Birds, descended from theropod dinosaurs, have feathers, a beak and hard-shelled eggs.
layers.deeper: The amniotic egg freed vertebrates from water. Bird bones are light and air-sacs give efficient breathing.
layers.expert: Birds (≈ 11,000 species) are a clade within Reptilia as phylogenetically defined. Feathers evolved before flight, probably for insulation and display.

layers.basics: Mammals have hair, three middle-ear bones and mammary glands. The three groups are monotremes (egg-laying), marsupials and placentals.
layers.deeper: Primates have grasping hands, forward-facing eyes and large brains; they include lemurs, monkeys, apes and humans.
layers.expert: Most living placental orders diversified after the end-Cretaceous extinction, though the timing is debated. There are about 6,500–6,700 mammal species (the count depends on the checklist) and ≈ 500 primates; roughly a quarter of assessed mammals are threatened.

title: Zoology field methods and identification
summary: How animals are surveyed and named.

layers.basics: Zoologists identify species with keys, specimens, photos and DNA barcodes, and count animals with transects, traps and cameras.
layers.deeper: The COI gene is the standard animal barcode (≈ 650 bp). Mark–recapture estimates population size.
layers.expert: Lincoln–Petersen: N ≈ (M·C)/R, where M is the number of animals marked on the first visit, C the number caught on the second visit and R the number of marked animals among them. It assumes a closed population, equal catchability and no mark loss. Occupancy models separate detection from presence. Specimen collection follows permits, ethics and museum curation standards.

title: Plant biology
summary: How plants are built, move water, make food, grow and respond.

layers.basics: Plants are living factories that capture sunlight. They have roots, stems and leaves, move water from soil to air, and respond to light, gravity and seasons.
layers.deeper: Xylem carries water up and phloem carries sugars around. Hormones such as auxin, gibberellin and ethylene coordinate growth, flowering and fruit ripening.
layers.expert: Plant physiology blends biophysics (water potential, cohesion–tension) with molecular signalling and development. C4 and CAM adaptations address the Rubisco oxygenase problem in warm, dry settings.

title: Plant body and tissues
summary: Roots, stems, leaves and their tissues.

layers.basics: Roots anchor and absorb, stems support and transport, leaves capture light. Dermal, ground and vascular tissues form the plant body.
layers.deeper: Meristems at tips (apical) and sides (lateral) allow growth throughout life. Secondary growth makes wood and bark.
layers.expert: Monocots have scattered vascular bundles; eudicots have them in a ring. Annual rings result from seasonal cambial activity and are used in dendrochronology.

title: Leaf anatomy and stomata
summary: Built for light, CO2 and water balance.

layers.basics: Leaves are thin and flat to catch light. Stomata (pores flanked by guard cells) let CO2 in and water vapour out.
layers.deeper: Guard cells open in light by taking up K+ and water, and close in drought via abscisic acid. A leaf loses ≈ 400 water molecules for each CO2 fixed (C3).
layers.expert: Stomatal density and index record past CO2 levels. Trade-off between carbon gain and water loss shapes plant strategies and water-use efficiency.

title: Water transport: xylem and cohesion–tension

layers.basics: Water evaporating from leaves pulls a continuous column of water up through the xylem from the roots.
layers.deeper: Cohesion between water molecules and adhesion to xylem walls support the column. Water flows from high to low water potential.
layers.expert: Cohesion–tension theory predicts negative xylem pressures, typically around −1 to −3 MPa depending on species and dryness; cavitation (embolism) is a risk in drought. Water potential Ψ = Ψs + Ψp, plus a gravity term Ψg ≈ 0.01 MPa per metre of height that matters in tall trees.

facts: ≈ −1 to −3 MPa (typical; varies with species and dryness)

title: Phloem and pressure-flow
summary: Moving sugars from source to sink.

layers.basics: Phloem carries sugars from leaves (sources) to roots, fruits and growing tips (sinks).
layers.deeper: Sugar loading raises osmotic pressure at the source so water enters; at the sink sugar leaves and water follows, driving bulk flow (Münch pressure-flow).
layers.expert: Phloem sap flows ≈ 0.5–1 m/h in sieve tubes; in apoplastic loaders, companion cells load sucrose using H⁺-coupled symporters; many other plants load through plasmodesmata instead. Aphid stylets sample phloem sap.

layers.basics: Plants need nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium and micronutrients from soil. Legumes host nitrogen-fixing bacteria in root nodules.
layers.deeper: Mycorrhizae extend root reach. Soil pH and structure control nutrient availability.
layers.expert: Rhizobia fix N₂ via nitrogenase at ≈ 100–200 kg N/ha/yr in good legume stands. Haber–Bosch fertiliser supports ≈ half of the world's food nitrogen. Carnivorous plants supplement N in poor soils.

layers.basics: In hot, dry places some plants concentrate CO2 around Rubisco. C4 plants (corn, sugarcane) separate steps in space; CAM plants (cacti, pineapple) separate them in time.
layers.deeper: Photorespiration, a wasteful side reaction of Rubisco with oxygen, costs C3 plants a notable share of their fixed carbon, more so at high temperature. C4 uses PEP carboxylase in mesophyll and the Calvin cycle in bundle sheath.
layers.expert: C4 evolved independently > 60 times; ≈ 3% of plant species, ≈ 25% of terrestrial primary production. CAM opens stomata at night. Engineering C4 rice is an active project.

title: Plant hormones
summary: Chemical signals for growth and development.

layers.basics: Auxin steers growth towards light; gibberellins promote stem elongation and germination; cytokinins promote cell division; abscisic acid closes stomata; ethylene ripens fruit.
layers.deeper: Apical dominance is auxin-mediated. Ripe apples release ethylene that ripens neighbours.
layers.expert: Auxin transport by PIN proteins creates gradients (chemiosmotic polar transport). Hormone receptors include TIR1 (auxin) and ETR1 (ethylene).

title: Tropisms, photoperiodism and plant defences

layers.basics: Plants bend toward light (phototropism) and roots grow down (gravitropism). Flowering time in many plants is set by the length of day and night (the uninterrupted dark period), sensed by photoreceptors such as phytochrome and cryptochrome.
layers.deeper: Plants defend with thorns, toxins and signals; attacked plants release volatile compounds; neighbours can detect them and prime their own defences, although whether this evolved as a signal to neighbours is debated.
layers.expert: Phytochromes switch between Pr and Pfr forms by red/far-red light; the FT protein is the mobile "florigen". Systemic acquired resistance involves salicylic acid.

open_questions: Whether plant volatile signals evolved to warn neighbours, and how common the effect is outside controlled experiments, is debated.

title: Plant reproduction and flowers

layers.basics: Flowers are reproductive organs. Pollen carries sperm to the ovule; after double fertilisation the ovule becomes a seed and the ovary becomes a fruit.
layers.deeper: Pollen is moved by animals (insects, birds, bats) or by wind. Fruits aid seed dispersal; plants can also reproduce asexually (runners, cloning).
layers.expert: Self-incompatibility systems prevent selfing. Seed dormancy and germination are controlled by abscisic acid and gibberellin. Agriculture exploits vegetative propagation and grafting.

facts: Share of global crop production from animal-pollinated crop types
dust-like; about 0.3 mm long in one Orchis species

title: Plant development and the ABC model

layers.basics: A seedling grows from a seed by cell division at meristems, and flowers form when a shoot meristem switches to reproductive development.
layers.deeper: In the ABC model, combinations of three gene classes decide sepals, petals, stamens and carpels.
layers.expert: Arabidopsis and snapdragon mutants (apetala2, pistillata, agamous, deficiens) led to the model; the B, C and E functions are MADS-box genes, and the class A function is clear only in Arabidopsis. Plant development is plastic and modular, with indeterminate growth.
